messages.subject: Perform Joint Approximate Diagonalization (JAD) on a set of matrices
parts:
Dear all,

does anybody have information about Blind Source Separation Solution(s)
in STAN? I am particular interested in the JAD (Joint Approximate Diagonalization)
Algorithm defined by Cardoso 

Link to cardoso Paper of JAD

or as variant in an Matlab implementation here:

http://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/32608-blind-modal-identification--bmid--toolbox/content/bmid_pkg/jad.m

There are some variants and since it is a fundamental algorithm,
it lets me hope that anybody have done some work already.

I would also like to ask how to solve the following transformation in STAN efficiently?

  eg<-eigen(solve(cov(X)))
  W<-(eg$vectors%*%diag(eg$values^0.5)) %*% solve(eg$vectors)

I thought about sampling cor(X) with:
L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2.0);
doing a scaling to archive cov(X).

I'm unsure, if there is not a way around in STAN to sample the eigenvalues directly,
to save a lot of simulation time.

Thank you,
Andre

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Perform Joint Approximate Diagonalization (JAD) on a set of matrices
parts:
On Wednesday, June 8, 2016 at 9:24:26 PM UTC-4, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
As a special case, I want to mimic the behavior of plsregress of Matlab which do a regression in PCA space. 
No limiting to PCA, I wanted to use JAD. 
Back to your question what it buy me in STAN, is the eigenvectors. I don't see how to directly sample
them in STAN.

Well, if you declare

matrix[K, K] Z;
vector<lower=0> d;

in the parameters block and do

matrix[K, K] Sigma;
{
  matrix[K, K] Q;
  Q <- qr_Q(Z);
  Sigma <- quad_form_diag(Q, d);
}

in transformed parameters block and do

to_vector(Z) ~ normal(0,1);

in the model block, that implies that Q is a priori uniformally distributed among orthogonal matrices. Then you can put any prior you want on d, which along with Q characterizes your prior beliefs about Sigma.

Ben

On Thursday, June 9, 2016 at 1:28:08 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Could we use this to build an orthogonal (or even
orthonormal) matrix data type?  It seems like
the unit normal trick is just like the unit vector
trick in that it should identify Z.
I don't know if it is the highest priority, but sure.

Do we then
need the Jacobian of qr_Q to allow us to put a prior
on Q?  Or is there a way to put a sensible prior on
Z that implies something reasonable for Q as in the
LKJ case?

A standard normal prior on the elements of Z implies Q is jointly uniform among matrices where Q'Q = I, which is often reasonable. Someone could then add an informative prior on Q in the model block without having to do a(nother) Jacobian, but I have never heard of anyone propose an informative prior for an orthogonal matrix.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Perform Joint Approximate Diagonalization (JAD) on a set of matrices
parts:
Ben,

instead of in 
Sigma <- quad_form_diag(Q, d);

matrix quad_form_diag(matrix m, vector v)
The quadratic form using the column vector v as a diagonal matrix, i.e.,
diag_matrix(v) * m * diag_matrix(v).

which results to:
> d%*%Q%*%d
            [,1]        [,2]        [,3]         [,4]
[1,] -0.16274514 -0.02647899  0.03445556  0.001797719
[2,]  0.03081396 -1.04807387  0.24288854 -0.027926451
[3,] -0.01518471 -0.33094556 -0.60159561  0.031659160
[4,]  0.00366433 -0.01226056  0.03678136  0.007972295

which is not symmetric, shouldn't it be: 
> Q%*%d%*%t(Q)
            [,1]       [,2]        [,3]        [,4]
[1,]  0.41132402 0.05321325 -0.02808319  0.01246768
[2,]  0.05321325 0.97448996  0.15714299  0.20198151
[3,] -0.02808319 0.15714299  0.75855923 -0.24647756
[4,]  0.01246768 0.20198151 -0.24647756  0.26838350

which is symmetric.

Let's assume a 2x2 covariance matrix. Then we would need 3 parameters.
However to_vector(Z) ~ normal(0,1) would require 4 parameters and
2 parameters for d.
Is this ok?

Andre

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Perform Joint Approximate Diagonalization (JAD) on a set of matrices
parts:
On Thursday, June 9, 2016 at 11:54:09 AM UTC-4, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
Ben,

instead of in 
Sigma <- quad_form_diag(Q, d);

matrix quad_form_diag(matrix m, vector v)
The quadratic form using the column vector v as a diagonal matrix, i.e.,
diag_matrix(v) * m * diag_matrix(v).

Yeah, I get tripped up by the names. Conceptually, Q * D * Q' is

Sigma <- quad_form(diag_matrix(d), transpose(Q));

but that may or may not be faster. You could declare d_sqrt to be the square roots of the eigenvalues and do

Sigma <- crossprod(diag_post_multiply(Q, d_sqrt));

Let's assume a 2x2 covariance matrix. Then we would need 3 parameters.
However to_vector(Z) ~ normal(0,1) would require 4 parameters and
2 parameters for d.
Is this ok?

Yes that is okay. Merely counting parameters neglects the prior information you impart about them. The effective number of parameters should be about the same either way.

Ben


Andre
